gloss: foot, leg; step, pace; time (occurrence); go about on foot: spy out, slander
summary: The foot and leg, of man, beast or the legs of a table: what a man stands on and walks with. So the feet are a man's going and his conduct (“a lamp to my foot is your word”), the ground a sole treads is ground taken and held (“every place the sole of your foot treads shall be yours”), and what is put under the feet is subdued (“till I make your enemies a footstool for your feet”); the people “at the feet” of a leader are those who follow him. רְגָלִים is also “times” (“three times you shall keep a feast to me in the year”). The verb, made from the noun, is to go about on foot: in the piel to spy out a land, or to go about slandering; Yahweh “taught Ephraim to walk”; and רַגְלִי is a man on foot, the footman beside the horseman. Arabic rijl “leg, foot” and rajila “go on foot”, Ugaritic riglu, Sabaean rgl “foot, leg; footsoldier”, Aramaic and Syriac רגלא give the same word.

words.summary: About 250 times, dual רַגְלַיִם for a pair. Its range runs from the limb itself (the leg as well as the foot: Lev 11:21; Ezk 1:7; Isa 7:20) through walking and conduct, treading and possession, subjection and following, to the count of “times”. Some of BDB's tokens for this key are רַגְלִי “footman” filed by spelling (Exo 12:37; 1Sa 4:10 and others), and the adjective's key takes several “my foot” (Psa 26:12; 94:18; 116:8) in exchange.

senses.definition: The foot and the whole leg of a man, a bird, a beast or a living creature in a vision; washed, shod and unshod, struck, lamed and bound; set beside the hand and the head as a part of the body.

evidence.note: “Let a little water be taken, and wash your feet (רַגְלֵיכֶם), and rest under the tree.”
“Eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot (רֶגֶל) for foot.”
Winged creeping things “that have legs (כְרָעַיִם) above their feet (לְרַגְלָיו), to leap with on the earth”.
“Their legs (רַגְלֵיהֶם) were a straight leg (רֶגֶל), and the sole of their feet like the sole of a calf's foot”: the whole leg, and its sole.
“From the sole of the foot (מִכַּף־רֶגֶל) even to the head there is no soundness in it.”
“Without you no man shall lift up his hand or his foot in all the land of Egypt.”
The dove “found no rest for the sole of her foot”.
Boils “from the sole of your foot to the crown of your head”.
Blood on the thumb of Aaron's right hand and the big toe of his right foot.
A priest with “a broken foot or a broken hand” may not draw near.
Mephibosheth, “lame of feet (נְכֵה רַגְלָיִם)”.
“Put off your sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (also Jos 5:15; quoted in Act 7:33).
The Passover eaten “with your sandals on your feet”.
“Your foot did not swell these forty years.”
Joseph: “they afflicted his foot with fetters”.
Of the table of the tabernacle: the rings at “the four corners that are at its four feet (רַגְלָיו)”, its legs.
See מַרְגְּלוֹת; the vision's feet like burnished bronze, as Ezk 1:7.

senses.gloss: foot as going: walking, journey, conduct
senses.definition: The feet as the means of going: to go on foot, to set out, to pass through; and so a man's way of life, where his feet run, turn, slip or are kept, often with דֶּרֶךְ, אֹרַח, נְתִיבָה and אַשּׁוּר “step” in parallel.

evidence.note: “Jacob lifted up his feet (וַיִּשָּׂא … רַגְלָיו) and went to the land of the sons of the east.”
“Only let me pass through on my feet (בְרַגְלָי).” Also Num 20:19.
“My son, do not walk in the way with them; withhold your foot (רַגְלְךָ) from their path.”
“For their feet run to evil and hasten to shed blood”, as Isa 59:7, quoted in Rom 3:15.
“Their feet are swift to shed blood.”
“Your word is a lamp to my foot (לְרַגְלִי) and a light to my path.”
“I considered my ways and turned my feet to your testimonies.”
“I have restrained my feet from every evil path, that I might keep your word.”
“Weigh the path of your foot, and let all your ways be established”; Heb 12:13 “make straight paths for your feet”.
“My foot has held fast to his steps (אֲשֻׁרוֹ); his way I have kept and not turned aside.”
“My feet had almost turned aside; my steps had nearly slipped.”
“He will guard the feet of his faithful ones, but the wicked shall be silent in darkness.”
“You have delivered my soul from death, have you not delivered my feet from stumbling, to walk before God in the light of the living?”
“He will not let your foot be moved.”
“He set my feet upon a rock, and established my steps.”
The strange woman: “her feet go down to death; her steps take hold of the grave (שְׁאוֹל)”.
“Guard your foot when you go to the house of God.”
“If you turn back your foot from the sabbath, from doing your pleasure on my holy day.”
“They have loved to wander; they have not restrained their feet.”
“How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news”: the messenger's coming (Nah 2:1; quoted in Rom 10:15).
Egypt, “where you sowed your seed and watered it with your foot”: the land's water moved by foot, unlike the rain of Canaan.
“I will no more make the foot of Israel wander from the land that I gave to their fathers.”
“I will lead on slowly, לְרֶגֶל הַמְּלָאכָה … וּלְרֶגֶל הַיְלָדִים”: at the pace of the cattle and of the children.
“Yahweh has blessed you לְרַגְלִי”: at my foot, wherever I went, since my coming; compare Arabic “in the time (رِجْل) of such a one”.
Jacob “gathered up his feet into the bed, and breathed his last, and was gathered to his people”.

senses.definition: Where the sole of the foot treads the land is entered and held; “not so much as the treading of the sole of a foot” is no possession at all.

evidence.note: “Every place on which the sole of your foot (כַּף־רַגְלְכֶם) treads shall be yours: from the wilderness and Lebanon, from the river, the river Euphrates, to the western sea.”
“Every place the sole of your foot treads upon, to you I have given it, as I said to Moses.”
“I will not give you of their land so much as the treading of the sole of a foot (מִדְרַךְ כַּף־רָגֶל), because I have given Mount Seir to Esau.”
“The land on which your foot has trodden shall be an inheritance to you and to your children for ever.”
Of Abraham: “he gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's length (βῆμα ποδός), and promised to give it to him for a possession and to his seed after him.”
When the soles of the priests' feet rest in the Jordan, its waters are cut off.

senses.definition: To put a thing or a people under the feet, or the feet on their necks, is to subdue them; to tread or trample with the feet is to crush or foul. The footstool (הֲדֹם רַגְלַיִם) is where the feet rest.

evidence.note: “Yahweh said to my lord, Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet (הֲדֹם לְרַגְלֶיךָ)”; quoted Mat 22:44; Act 2:34–35; Heb 1:13.
“You have put all things under his feet”; quoted 1Co 15:27; Eph 1:22; Heb 2:8.
“Come near, put your feet on the necks of these kings.”
“Until Yahweh put them under the soles of his feet.”
“They fell under my feet.”
“You shall tread down the wicked, for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet.”
“He subdues peoples under us, and nations under our feet.”
“The foot tramples it, the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy.”
“The crown of pride of the drunkards of Ephraim shall be trodden under feet.”
The fat sheep “trample the rest of your pastures with your feet … and foul the water with your feet”.
Kings and queens “shall lick the dust of your feet”.
The Aramaic: the fourth beast “trampled the rest with its feet”.

senses.gloss: the feet of God: his footstool, the place of his feet
senses.definition: Said of God appearing and dwelling among his people: what lies under his feet, the ark and the sanctuary as his footstool and “the place of my feet”, and the earth as his footstool.

evidence.note: “They saw the God of Israel, and under his feet as it were a work of sapphire brick.”
“To build a house of rest for the ark of the covenant of Yahweh, and for the footstool of the feet of our God.”
“Let us go into his dwelling; let us worship at his footstool.”
“Exalt Yahweh our God, and worship at his footstool; holy is he.”
He “did not remember his footstool in the day of his anger”.
“To beautify the place of my sanctuary, and I will make the place of my feet glorious.”
“The place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet, where I will dwell in the midst of the sons of Israel for ever.”
“The heavens are my throne, and the earth is my footstool”; quoted by Stephen, Act 7:49.
“His feet shall stand in that day on the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east.”
“He bowed the heavens and came down, and thick darkness was under his feet.”
“The clouds are the dust of his feet.”

senses.gloss: at the feet: following; falling at the feet
senses.definition: The people “at the feet” (בְּרַגְלָיו, לְרַגְלָיו) of a leader are those who go after him; to fall at someone's feet is to beg or to do homage; to sit at the feet is to receive his words.

evidence.note: “Go out, you and all the people who are at your feet (בְּרַגְלֶיךָ).”
“Ten thousand men went up at his feet”: followed Barak.
Abigail rode, “with five of her maidens who went at her feet (לְרַגְלָהּ)”.
“The king went out, and all his household at his feet.”
“Loaves of bread to the people who are at my feet.”
“Who stirred up one from the east, whom righteousness calls to its foot (לְרַגְלוֹ)?”
Abigail “fell at his feet and said, On me, my lord, be the iniquity”.
The Shunammite “fell at his feet and bowed to the ground, and took up her son”.
Esther “fell down at his feet and wept and begged him”.
“All his holy ones are in your hand, and they sat down at your feet; each receives of your words”; compare Luk 10:39, Mary “sat at the Lord's feet and heard his word”.
Mary “fell at his feet”, as 1Sa 25:24.

senses.definition: The plural רְגָלִים with a number: so many times, as steps are counted.

evidence.note: “Three times (שָׁלֹשׁ רְגָלִים) you shall keep a feast to me in the year”; listed in the next verses as Unleavened Bread, Harvest and Ingathering.
The donkey: “What have I done to you, that you have struck me these three times?”

senses.definition: “Feet” in phrases that speak modestly of the body: to cover the feet is to relieve oneself, “water of the feet” is urine, “hair of the feet” is the body's hair below, and what comes “from between the feet” is the afterbirth.

evidence.note: Eglon's servants: “Surely he is covering his feet in the cool room.”
“Saul went in to cover his feet” in the cave.
“To eat their own dung and drink their own water of the feet (מֵימֵי רַגְלֵיהֶם)”, the Qere (also Isa 36:12).
“The Lord will shave with a razor … the head and the hair of the feet, and it shall also consume the beard.”
“Her afterbirth that comes out from between her feet.”
“You spread your feet to everyone who passed by.”

evidence.locator: Psa.110.1, לְרַגְלֶיךָ → ποδῶν; Isa.66.1, רַגְלָי → ποδῶν; Deu.2.5, רָגֶל → ποδός; Isa.52.7, רַגְלֵי → πόδες; πούς renders רֶגֶל ×169

evidence.note: Psa 110:1, “till I put your enemies under your feet (ποδῶν)”.
“Not even a foot's length (βῆμα ποδός)”, Deu 2:5.
“How beautiful are the feet (πόδες)”, Isa 52:7.
“His feet (πόδες) like burnished bronze”, as Dan 10:6; Ezk 1:7.

parallels.note: Hand and foot together for the whole body and its doings.
From the sole of the foot to the head: the whole body.
The step, beside the foot in describing a man's going.

phrases.gloss: under his feet, subject to him

words.gloss: go about on foot: spy out; go about slandering; (tiphil) teach to walk
words.summary: A verb made from the foot: to go about on foot, and so to go through a land to see it (spy), or to go about with tales (slander). The tiphil תִּרְגַּלְתִּי (Hos 11:3) is to make to go on foot, to teach to walk. The Phoenician piel “move” may be the same verb.

senses.definition: With עַל־לְשֹׁנוֹ: to go about with the tongue, spreading tales against a neighbour.

evidence.note: Who shall dwell on your holy hill? He who “does not go about (רָגַל) on his tongue, does no evil to his neighbour, nor takes up a reproach against his near one”: the parallels fix it as slander.

senses.gloss: spy out, explore (a land, a city); (participle) spies
senses.definition: To go through a land or city on foot to see it and bring word back; the participle מְרַגְּלִים is spies, men sent secretly, as Joseph accused his brothers of being.

evidence.note: “You are spies (מְרַגְּלִים); to see the nakedness of the land you have come.”
Joshua sent “two men, spies, secretly, saying, Go, see the land and Jericho”.
The Danites sent five men “to spy out the land and to search it (לְרַגֵּל … וּלְחָקְרָהּ)”.
“Moses sent to spy out Jazer, and they took its villages.”
They came to the valley of Eshcol “and spied it out”.
Rahab “hid the messengers whom Joshua sent to spy out Jericho”; Heb 11:31, she “received the spies (κατασκόπους) in peace”.
“Go up and spy out the land; and the men went up and spied out Ai.”
Caleb: “Moses sent me from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land.”
“David sent out spies, and knew that Saul had come.”
“To search the city, and to spy it out, and to overthrow it” (also 1Ch 19:3).
Absalom “sent spies (מְרַגְּלִים) through all the tribes of Israel”: secret messengers.

senses.definition: With בְּ: to go about against someone with false report.

evidence.note: Mephibosheth of Ziba: “He has slandered (וַיְרַגֵּל) your servant to my lord the king.”

senses.gloss: teach to walk, set on his feet
senses.definition: To make a child go on its feet, holding it.

evidence.note: “And I taught Ephraim to walk (תִרְגַּלְתִּי), taking them by their arms; but they did not know that I healed them”: a father with a child (Hos 11:1).

evidence.locator: Gen.42.9, מְרַגְּלִים → κατάσκοποί; κατάσκοπος renders the piel participle ×8, κατασκοπεύω and κατασκέπτομαι the finite verb

evidence.note: “By faith Rahab the harlot did not perish with the disobedient, having received the spies (κατασκόπους) in peace”: the מְרַגְּלִים of Jos 2:1; 6:25.
False brothers “who came in secretly to spy out (κατασκοπῆσαι) our freedom”.

words.summary: The foot with the -ִי of belonging: one on foot. Always after a number of men, the people or soldiers who go on foot, set against the horsemen and chariots. Its BDB key also takes several רַגְלִי “my foot” (Psa 26:12; 38:17; 94:18; 116:8; Job 23:11; 31:5), which are the noun.

senses.definition: Men going on foot, counted: Israel leaving Egypt, the men of an army, the footmen beside horsemen and chariots.

evidence.note: “About six hundred thousand men on foot (רַגְלִי), besides children.”
“The people among whom I am are six hundred thousand on foot.”
“If you have run with footmen (רַגְלִים) and they have wearied you, how will you contend with horses?”
“David took from him seventeen hundred horsemen and twenty thousand footmen (אִישׁ רַגְלִי).”
Chariots, horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen.
“Fifty horsemen and ten chariots and ten thousand footmen.”
“Four hundred thousand footmen who drew the sword.”

words.summary: The Aramaic of Daniel: the feet of the image in Nebuchadnezzar's dream, and the feet of the beasts of Daniel's vision.

senses.definition: The feet of the image, part iron and part clay, which the stone strikes; the feet of the first beast, stood up like a man; the feet with which the fourth beast tramples.

evidence.note: “Its legs of iron, its feet (רַגְלוֹהִי) part of iron and part of clay.”
“A stone was cut out without hands, and struck the image on its feet of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces.”
“The feet and toes, part potter's clay and part iron: it shall be a divided kingdom.”
The lion-like beast “was made to stand on two feet like a man, and a man's heart was given to it”.
The fourth beast “devoured and broke in pieces, and trampled the rest with its feet (בְּרַגְלַהּ)”.

words.gloss: the place at the feet; the feet
words.summary: A plural of place made from the foot, as מְרַאֲשׁוֹת is the place at the head (1Sa 26:7): where the feet lie, and so the feet themselves.

senses.gloss: the place at the feet; the feet
senses.definition: The place at the feet of one lying down, which Ruth uncovered and where she lay; in Daniel's vision, the feet (or legs) of the man clothed in linen.

evidence.note: “Go in and uncover the place of his feet (מַרְגְּלֹתָיו) and lie down.”
“Behold, a woman lying at his feet.”
“She lay at his feet until the morning.”
“His arms and his feet like the gleam of burnished bronze”: Rev 1:15, “his feet like fine bronze”.

words.summary: The Peshitta's word for πούς throughout the New Testament (about a hundred times), carrying the Hebrew's uses: washing and anointing the feet, falling and sitting at the feet, the feet of the messenger, enemies put under the feet.

senses.definition: The foot, with the Hebrew idioms of the Old Testament passages it quotes.

evidence.note: Psa 110:1, “under your feet (רֵגְלַיכּ)”.
“A footstool (כֻּובְשָא) for your feet.”
“He has subjected all things under his feet.”
“The God of peace will crush the adversary (סָטָנָא) under your feet shortly.”
“How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of peace”, Isa 52:7.
“To direct our feet into the way of peace.”
Mary “sat at the feet of our Lord and heard his words”, as Deu 33:3.
Paul, brought up “at the feet of Gamaliel”.
He began “to wash the feet of his disciples”.
“Not even the treading of a foot (דֻּורכּתָֿא דּרֵגֿלָא)”, Deu 2:5.
The risen Jesus: “See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself; handle me and see, for a spirit has not flesh and bones as you see that I have.”

words.summary: One who goes on foot, as Hebrew רַגְלִי; once in the Peshitta.

senses.definition: The soldiers on foot, set beside the horsemen.

evidence.note: “The next day the horsemen dismissed the foot-soldiers (לרַגָּלֵא) their companions to return to the camp.”

words.summary: Once in the Peshitta, for χείμαρρος, the brook Kidron. How a stream comes from the foot is not shown by scripture; Arabic rijl is also “a canal of a river”, and the places רֹגְלִים and עֵין רֹגֵל are named from the same letters.

evidence.note: Jesus went out with his disciples “across the brook (דַּרגֵֿלתָּא) of Kidron, where there was a garden”.

cognates.gloss: leg, foot; a part or share of a thing; a time (in the time of); a swarm of locusts; a canal of a river
cognates.note: The leg and foot, opposed to يَد “hand”, as רֶגֶל and יָד are paired. Its extended senses run close to the Hebrew's: كَانَ ذٰلِكَ عَلَى رِجْلِ فُلَانٍ “that was in the time of such a one” beside לְרַגְלִי (Gen 30:30) and רְגָלִים “times”; and رِجْلُ بَحْرٍ “a canal of a river” beside the Syriac “brook”.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 1044, art. رجل, رِجْلٌ (n14927)
evidence.note: “The leg of a human being and of a bird … the foot of a man … رِجْلُ الإِنْسَانِ that with which the man walks … A canal of a river … A part, or portion, of a thing … A swarm … of locusts … A time. One says, كَانَ ذٰلِكَ عَلَى رِجْلِ فُلَانٍ That was in the time of such a one; in his life-time.”

evidence.locator: SEM000350 rgl [leg], ARB010400 rijol [Foot], HEB006778 regel [foot]

cognates.gloss: go on foot, having no beast to ride; (rājil) one on foot, a footman, opposite of a horseman
cognates.note: The verb from the foot, as Hebrew רָגַל: going about on foot. rājil “footman, the opposite of فَارِس horseman” is רַגְלִי set against the horsemen (2Sa 8:4).

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 1043, art. رجل, رَجِلَ (n14921)
evidence.note: “He (a man) went on foot, in a journey, by himself, having no beast whereon to ride … ترجّل he went on foot … ارتجل he went on his legs, or feet, for the purpose of accomplishing the object of his want.”

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 1046, art. رجل, رَاجِلٌ (n14951)
evidence.note: “Going, or a goer, on foot; a pedestrian; a footman; the opposite of فَارِسٌ.”

cognates.note: Known from the syllabic (cuneiform) spelling at Ugarit, of the base /rigl-/; the alphabetic texts' usual word for the foot is pʿn, as Hebrew פַּעַם.
Both Hebrew words in one South Arabian root: the foot or leg of a wounded man, and the footsoldier set beside the mounted man (“one mounted man and three footsoldiers”), as רֶגֶל and רַגְלִי.

evidence.note: “FOOT, LEG [Ar rijl] … ‘disease of his feet/legs’ … ‘the injury which affected his foot’ … FOOTSOLDIER [cf Ar rājil “(one who goes) on foot”] … ‘(one) mounted man and three footsoldiers’.”

cognates.gloss: foot, leg; pace; (transferred) good or bad luck coming in one's wake; festival
cognates.note: The Targums' word for the foot; the Targum of Gen 33:14 renders לְרֶגֶל “at the pace of” with it, and the Palestinian Targum of Gen 30:30 uses it for the blessing that came “at my foot”.

evidence.note: “foot, leg; pace. Targ. Lev. XXI, 19. Targ. Gen. XXXIII, 14 … Trnsf. good or bad luck coming in the wake of. Targ. Y. Gen. XXX, 30.”

cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic: the verb “move, run” and the footman of the Targums, which renders Hebrew רַגְלִי in Exo 12:37, Num 11:21 and Jer 12:5.

evidence.note: “to move, run … Af. to lead; to accustom.”
“= h. רַגְלִי, footman. Targ. O. Ex. XII, 37 … Targ. O. Num. XI, 21 … Targ. Jer. XII, 5.”

cognates.note: The Peshitta's root: the foot (about a hundred times, for πούς), the foot-soldier (Act 23:32), and the brook (Jhn 18:1). SEDRA's verb “dismount” has no token in the New Testament.

evidence.locator: root 1728 RGL; lexemes 2932 RGL (dismount), 2933 RGLA (foot), 2934 RGLA (foot soldier), 2935 RGLTA (brook)

cognates.note: The dictionary's root entry refers to a noun mrgl “footman” that its M section does not contain in the copy consulted, and cites no text for the verb.

evidence.note: “v. pi'el MOVE: See MRGL, ‘footman.’”

cognates.note: Ethiopic's word for the foot is commonly taken as the same word with its letters moved (*rigl > ʾəgr); the change is argued, not shown, and Dillmann has not been consulted.

evidence.note: “foot, foot (the measurement), ray of sunshine, prow”; “metathesized from Proto-Semitic *rigl-”.

doctrine.statement: David writes, “Yahweh said to my lord, Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet” (Psa 110:1), and of man, “you have put all things under his feet” (Psa 8:7). Jesus asks how David's son can be David's lord (Mat 22:44). Peter says that David “did not ascend into the heavens”, but said this of Jesus, whom God raised and exalted (Act 2:32–35). Paul sets the two psalms together: Christ “must reign till he has put all enemies under his feet; the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death”, and “when he says all things are put under him, it is plain that he is excepted who put all things under him”, so that at the end “the Son himself shall be subject to him who put all things under him, that God may be all in all” (1Co 15:25–28). Hebrews adds, “now we do not yet see all things put under him, but we see Jesus … crowned with glory and honour” (Heb 2:8–9), “from that time waiting till his enemies are made a footstool for his feet” (Heb 10:12–13). From the verses: Yahweh and David's lord are two, the one giving and the other receiving; the man Jesus sits at God's right hand waiting; the subjection is not yet complete, and is completed when death itself is destroyed in the resurrection; and the Son is then subject to the Father. David himself is not in heaven but awaits that resurrection.

Israel was told, “every place on which the sole of your foot treads shall be yours”, with the borders named (Deu 11:24; Jos 1:3), and Caleb was promised “the land on which your foot has trodden … for ever” (Jos 14:9). Abraham was told to walk through the land “for to you I will give it” (Gen 13:15, 17). Stephen says that God “gave him no inheritance in it, not even the treading of a foot, yet promised to give it to him for a possession and to his seed after him” (Act 7:5, from Deu 2:5's phrase), and Hebrews says that Abraham and his sons “died in faith, not having received the promises” (Heb 11:13), looking for the city that has foundations (Heb 11:10). From the verses: the promise is of the land itself, ground that feet tread, made to Abraham personally; he never held a foot of it; so the promise waits to be kept to him, which requires his resurrection.

In Nebuchadnezzar's dream a stone “cut out without hands … struck the image on its feet of iron and clay and broke them in pieces”, and “the stone that struck the image became a great mountain and filled the whole earth” (Dan 2:34–35). Daniel explains, “in the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed … it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever” (Dan 2:44). Zechariah says of the day of Yahweh, “his feet shall stand in that day on the Mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east”, and “Yahweh shall be king over all the earth” (Zec 14:4, 9). Jesus was taken up from the Mount of Olives, and the angels said, “this same Jesus … shall so come in like manner as you saw him go into heaven” (Act 1:11–12). From the verses: the kingdom of God strikes the last form of the kingdoms of men at its feet and replaces them on the earth, which it fills; and the place where the feet of the returning Jesus stand is on the earth, at Jerusalem.

When the dead man touched the bones of Elisha “he revived and stood up on his feet” (2Ki 13:21), and in the valley of dry bones “breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up on their feet, an exceedingly great army” (Ezk 37:10), which Yahweh explains, “I will open your graves … and bring you into the land of Israel” (Ezk 37:12). The risen Jesus said, “See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself; handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have”, and showed them his hands and his feet (Luk 24:39–40). From the verses: resurrection is the dead body made to live and stand again on its feet, not a spirit leaving it; the one raised is the same person, with hands and feet.

Open questions: (1) how the verb's senses spy / slander come from the foot is inferred (going about on foot, Arabic rajila) rather than shown by a verse; the Septuagint's ἐδόλωσεν (Psa 15:3) and μεθώδευσεν (2Sa 19:28) are renderings only.
